definition: A disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter.
A wave where the oscillations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer. Examples: light, water waves, all EM waves.
A wave where the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Example: sound waves.
The maximum displacement of a point on a wave from its rest position. Measured in metres (m). Larger amplitude = more energy.
The distance between two successive identical points on a wave, e.g. crest to crest or compression to compression. Symbol: λ, measured in metres (m).
The number of complete waves passing a point per second. Symbol: f, measured in hertz (Hz).
The time taken for one complete wave to pass a point. T = 1/f. Measured in seconds (s).
The speed at which a wave travels through a medium. Calculated using: v = fλ (wave speed = frequency × wavelength). Measured in m/s.
The highest point of a transverse wave, where displacement is at its maximum positive value.
The lowest point of a transverse wave, where displacement is at its maximum negative value.
A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are pushed closer together, creating a high-pressure region.
A region in a longitudinal wave where particles are spread further apart, creating a low-pressure region.
The bouncing of a wave off a surface. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. The wave changes direction but not speed or frequency.
The angle between the incoming wave (or ray) and the normal to the surface at the point of incidence.
The angle between the reflected wave (or ray) and the normal to the surface. Always equals the angle of incidence.
An imaginary line drawn perpendicular to a surface at the point where a wave meets it. Angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal.
The change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium to another, caused by a change in wave speed.
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal at the point where the wave enters the new medium.
A property of a medium that determines how fast light travels through it. A denser medium slows light down more and causes greater refraction.
When a wave travelling in a denser medium hits the boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle and is completely reflected back into the medium.
The angle of incidence above which total internal reflection occurs. At this angle, the refracted ray travels along the boundary.
A longitudinal wave produced by vibrating objects that travels as compressions and rarefactions through a medium. Cannot travel through a vacuum.
How high or low a sound seems — determined by its frequency. Higher frequency = higher pitch.
How loud or quiet a sound seems — determined by its amplitude. Larger amplitude = louder sound.
Sound waves with a frequency above the upper limit of human hearing (above 20,000 Hz). Used in medical imaging and sonar.
A reflected sound wave. Used to measure distances — the time taken for an echo to return can be used to calculate the distance to a surface.
A device used to display waveforms of sound waves, showing amplitude, frequency and wave shape on a screen.
The family of transverse waves that all travel at the speed of light (3 × 10⁸ m/s) in a vacuum. Arranged in order of frequency/wavelength: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma.
The longest wavelength, lowest frequency part of the EM spectrum. Used for TV and radio broadcasting and satellite communication.
EM waves used in cooking (absorbed by water molecules) and in mobile phone and satellite communication.
EM waves emitted by all objects as heat. Used in thermal imaging cameras, remote controls, and optical fibre communication.
The narrow band of the EM spectrum that the human eye can detect. Ranges from red (longest wavelength) to violet (shortest wavelength).
EM waves with shorter wavelengths than visible light. Causes tanning and skin damage. Used in sterilisation and detecting forged banknotes.
High-frequency EM waves that pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone and dense materials. Used in medical imaging.
The shortest wavelength, highest frequency part of the EM spectrum. Emitted by radioactive nuclei. Used in cancer treatment and sterilising medical equipment.
The speed at which all EM waves travel in a vacuum: 3 × 10⁸ m/s (300,000,000 m/s).
Radiation with enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, creating ions. UV, X-rays and gamma rays are ionising. Can damage cells and DNA.
When a surface takes in the energy of a wave rather than reflecting or transmitting it. Dark, matt surfaces are good absorbers of infrared radiation.
When a wave passes through a material without being absorbed or reflected.
Radiation emitted by a perfect absorber and emitter of all wavelengths. The hotter the object, the more radiation emitted and the shorter the peak wavelength.
An object that gives out radiation. All objects emit infrared radiation — hotter objects emit more and at shorter wavelengths.
As the temperature of an object increases, the intensity of radiation emitted increases and the peak wavelength decreases (shifts towards shorter wavelengths).
